title: DSA in Python: two pointers, sliding window, stack, binary search
seriesDescription: Hashing, windows, stacks, binary search, lists, trees, heaps and graphs with Python code. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Python versions of the window, stack and binary search patterns: list and deque operations, the bisect module, the monotonic deque and the Python-specific cost traps.
source: Python documentation (bisect, collections.deque, list time complexity); LeetCode problem set; NeetCode roadmap

questions.prompt: Write a Python function max_area(h) for "container with most water": the bars at indices l and r hold min(h[l], h[r]) * (r - l) water. Use two pointers starting at both ends.

checks.label: starts two pointers at the two ends and loops while l < r
computes the area with min of the two heights
tracks the best with max
moves a pointer inward each step
returns the best area

questions.explanation: Always move the shorter bar: moving the taller one can only shrink the width without raising the limiting height.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function length_of_longest_substring(s) returning the length of the longest substring without repeating characters, using a sliding window and a dict of last-seen positions.

checks.label: keeps a dict of last-seen positions
walks the string with a right pointer
moves the left edge but never backwards (max with left)
measures the window as right - left + 1
tracks the best length

questions.explanation: The max(left, ...) is the part people forget: for "abba" the second a must not drag the left edge backwards.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function sliding_max(nums, k) returning the maximum of every window of size k, in O(n), using a deque of indices.
questions.starter:
from collections import deque

def sliding_max(nums, k):

checks.label: uses a deque
pops smaller values from the back
drops the front index when it leaves the window
appends the current index
records the maximum from the front once the first window is full

questions.explanation: The deque holds indices whose values decrease from front to back, so the front is always the window maximum. Each index enters and leaves once, hence O(n).

questions.prompt: Write a Python function is_valid(s) that returns True when every bracket in s made of ()[]{} is closed by the right type in the right order.

checks.label: uses a list (or deque) as a stack
pushes opening brackets
pops and compares on a closing bracket
maps bracket types to each other
returns whether the stack is empty at the end

questions.explanation: Check for an empty stack before popping, and require the stack to be empty at the end ("((" must fail).

questions.prompt: Write a Python function count_in_range(a, lo, hi) returning how many values x of the sorted list a satisfy lo <= x <= hi, using the bisect module (two O(log n) searches).
questions.starter:
import bisect

def count_in_range(a, lo, hi):

checks.label: uses bisect_left for the lower end
uses bisect_right (or bisect) for the upper end
subtracts the two insertion points
returns the count

questions.explanation: bisect_left(a, lo) is the first index with value >= lo and bisect_right(a, hi) is the first index with value > hi. The difference is the number of values in between.

questions.prompt: For a = [1, 2, 4, 4, 4, 7], what is bisect_right(a, 4) - bisect_left(a, 4)?
questions.explanation: bisect_left returns 2 and bisect_right returns 5, so the difference 3 is the number of copies of 4. I ran it to confirm.

questions.prompt: Match each Python expression with its effect.

right.text: Pushes x on top of a list-based stack
Removes and returns the last item, raising IndexError if empty
Reads the top of the stack without removing it
Removes and returns the first item of a deque in O(1)
Adds x at the front of a deque in O(1)

questions.explanation: A list is a fine stack because the end operations are O(1) amortised. For queues use collections.deque: list.pop(0) shifts every element and costs O(n).

questions.text: A plain list works as a stack: push with st.{1}(x), pop the top with st.{2}(), and peek at the top with st[{3}].
questions.explanation: All three are O(1). For a queue use deque.popleft() instead of pop(0).

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: In Python, mid = (lo + hi) // 2 cannot overflow, unlike the same expression in languages with fixed-width integers.

whys.a: Correct: the sum simply grows to a bigger integer, so the classic midpoint overflow bug does not exist in Python.
whys.b: R is exactly the reason, so it does explain A.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: You can mention the overflow-safe form lo + (hi - lo) // 2 anyway to show you know the issue when the interviewer asks about other languages.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: A monotonic stack finds the next greater element for every item of a list in O(n) total time.
questions.reason: list.append and list.pop at the end are O(1) amortised.

whys.a: R only covers the cost of one stack operation, not the total number of operations.
whys.b: Correct: both are true, but the linear bound comes from every index being pushed once and popped at most once; R alone does not give it.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Each element enters the stack once and leaves once, so the inner while loop does at most n pops across the whole scan.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: bisect.insort inserts a value into a sorted list in O(log n) total time.
questions.reason: bisect finds the insertion position in O(log n) comparisons.

whys.a: A is false, so no explanation can hold.
whys.b: A is false, so both-true options are out.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: R is true, but the list insert shifts later elements, so the whole insort is O(n); a heap or sorted container is the answer when you need many inserts.

questions.explanation: Finding the place is logarithmic; making room is linear. Do not claim O(log n) for insort in an interview.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Binary search on a sorted list with bisect needs the list to be sorted.
questions.reason: bisect sorts the list on every call.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false, so no both-true option applies.
whys.c: Correct: A is true (the result is meaningless on unsorted data), and R is false because bisect never sorts or checks the order.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: bisect trusts you. Sort once, then search many times.

questions.prompt: Using list.pop(0) to dequeue from a long Python list is O(n), so collections.deque with popleft() is preferred for queues.

options.why: Correct: popping the first item shifts every remaining item one place left.
It is linear: the list has to move the rest of its items.

questions.explanation: This is the reason BFS code uses deque. A deque pops from either end in O(1).

questions.prompt: list.append is O(n) in the worst case on every call, so a list is a poor stack.

options.why: Append is amortised constant time; occasional resizing is spread over many calls.
Correct: occasional resizing is amortised, so append and pop at the end are O(1) amortised.

questions.explanation: The occasional resize copies the buffer, but it happens rarely enough that the average cost per append is constant.

questions.prompt: A Python loop reads while lo <= hi: mid = (lo + hi) // 2; if a[mid] < target: lo = mid; else: hi = mid - 1. Which situation makes it loop forever?

options.text: a[mid] < target while mid == lo, e.g. lo = 0, hi = 1
options.why: Correct: lo = mid leaves lo unchanged, so the range never shrinks.

options.text: The list contains many repeated duplicate values in a row
options.why: Duplicates change which index is found, not whether the loop ends.

options.text: The target is smaller than every element in the whole list
options.why: hi keeps decreasing until it drops below lo, so the loop exits.

options.text: The list length happens to be an odd number of elements
options.why: Parity does not matter; the update rule for lo does.

questions.explanation: Use lo = mid + 1 for the "go right" branch (or switch to the half-open template). Always check that every branch shrinks the range.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Python's bisect module are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: bisect_left(a, x) returns the index of the leftmost position where x could be inserted keeping order.
options.why: Correct: it is the first index whose value is >= x.

options.text: bisect_right(a, x) returns an insertion point after any existing entries equal to x.
options.why: Correct: it is the first index whose value is > x.

options.text: bisect works on an unsorted list as long as the values are comparable.
options.why: False: the result is meaningless unless the list is sorted.

options.text: insort(a, x) inserts in O(log n) total time.
options.why: False: finding the spot is O(log n) but the insert shifts items, so it is O(n).

questions.explanation: Both functions run in O(log n) comparisons; use the key= argument (Python 3.10+) to search by a computed value.
